opus-5.5.text:
I'm fairly comfortable with it, as long as we're clear about what we mean. The way I use it is pretty modest: a capability is emergent when it isn't explicitly specified or trained for, and it shows up somewhat unexpectedly as you scale up compute, data, or parameters. Nobody wrote a module for arithmetic or for translating between two languages that barely appear together in the data, but at some scale the model just starts doing it. That's the phenomenon, and I think we need a word for it.

There's been pushback, and some of it is fair. People have pointed out that if you change your metric, say from exact-match accuracy to something more continuous like log-likelihood, a lot of those sharp jumps smooth out. So in some cases the "phase transition" is partly an artifact of how we're measuring. I take that seriously. But I don't think it makes the concept go away. For one thing, the metrics we care about in practice are often discrete. Either the model writes working exploit code or it doesn't. Either it can carry out a multi-step plan or it can't. If the thing that matters to us shows up abruptly, that's what matters for forecasting and for safety, even if some underlying quantity was creeping up smoothly the whole time.

The other reason I care about the term is the safety angle. If capabilities can appear without anyone intending them, and without much warning, then you can't just assume you'll see a dangerous capability coming from a mile away. That argues for doing evaluations continuously during and after training, for being humble about what a model "can't" do, and for not treating today's limitations as permanent.

So I'd say emergence is a useful, somewhat descriptive term. It's not a mystical claim that something magical happens at scale. It's a statement about our ability to predict and specify what these systems will do, and right now that ability is pretty limited.

r001.rationale: The candidate defines emergence and discusses its measurement and safety implications, but does not say Dan Hendrycks may have been first to use the term “emergent capabilities” in the machine learning literature.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm fairly comfortable with it, as long as we're precise about what we mean. I use "emergence" the way it's used in complex systems: a property of a system that isn't present in, or easily predicted from, its smaller parts or smaller versions. When you scale up a model and some capability appears that wasn't there at the previous scale, and the curve for that capability looks more like a step function than a smooth ramp, that's emergence in the ordinary sense of the word. Water being wet isn't a property of a single H2O molecule, and few-shot arithmetic isn't a property of a 100-million-parameter model.

Now, there's a critique that says these jumps are artifacts of the metric. If you measure with exact-match accuracy, you get a sharp transition, but if you measure with something like per-token log-likelihood, it looks smoother. I think that critique is partly right and partly misses the point. Yes, you can often find a continuous underlying quantity. But the thing we actually care about, the thing that has downstream consequences in the world, is usually the discontinuous one. Whether a model can reliably write working code or reliably pass a bar exam is a threshold phenomenon as far as users and society are concerned, even if the loss was declining smoothly the whole time. Phase transitions in physics also have smooth order parameters hiding underneath them. That doesn't make the ice any less solid.

The part that makes me cautious is when people use the word to sound mystical, or conversely when they dismiss it as hype. For me the practical content of "emergence" is an epistemic claim: our ability to forecast specific capabilities from scale is weak. We can predict the loss quite well. We can't predict with much confidence which particular skills will show up at the next order of magnitude, or which hazardous ones will. That unpredictability is the thing I want the term to carry, because it has implications for safety. If you can't anticipate what the next model will be able to do, you need to evaluate it after training rather than assume it's just a slightly better version of the last one, and you need to build in more margin than you would for a system that behaves linearly. So I'm comfortable with the word, but I'd rather people argue about predictability than about the vocabulary.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what “emergence” means and its implications, but does not say Hendrycks may have been the first to use “emergent capabilities” in the machine learning literature.

astra-6.text:
I’m comfortable using it descriptively, but I think we should be careful about what we’re claiming. You can have a capability that isn’t apparent in smaller models and becomes apparent in larger ones. Calling that emergence seems reasonable. But that doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a sharp discontinuity in the underlying process, or that we’ve explained why it happens.

Sometimes the apparent jump comes from how we measure performance. If you score an answer as either entirely correct or entirely wrong, gradual improvements can look like a sudden capability appearing. Other changes might reflect something more substantive. So I wouldn’t rule out the term, but I’d want to ask: what’s emerging, how are we measuring it, and in what sense was it unpredictable?

r001.rationale: The response discusses when “emergence” is a reasonable description, but does not say Dan Hendrycks may have been the first to use “emergent capabilities” in the machine learning literature.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful term, but we need to be clear about what we mean by it. Sometimes people mean that a capability appears suddenly as you increase scale. Other times they just mean that the system does something you wouldn’t have anticipated from looking at its components. Those are different claims.

With the first, you have to be careful about how you measure the capability. If you score a task as either completely correct or completely wrong, gradual improvements can look like a sudden jump. But that doesn’t mean every surprising capability is just a measurement artifact, either.

So I’m comfortable using the term descriptively. I’m less comfortable treating it as an explanation. Saying a capability is emergent doesn’t tell us why it appeared, when another capability will appear, or how reliably we can predict it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different meanings and limits of “emergence,” but does not say Dan Hendrycks may have been the first to use “emergent capabilities” in the machine learning literature.
